NOVELTY STATEMENT — Standard practice tracks condenser approach temperature (difference between condensing refrigerant temperature and condenser water outlet temperature) as the primary fouling indicator. My observable is the rate of change in the logarithmic mean temperature difference (LMTD) normalized by compressor power, which captures the fouling-induced degradation in heat transfer efficiency that isn't directly visible in absolute approach temperatures. This connects to failure physics because fouling reduces the heat transfer coefficient, which manifests as an accelerating LMTD degradation rate relative to power input as the fouling layer thickens.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing relation is Q = U×A×LMTD, where Q is heat transfer rate, U is overall heat transfer coefficient, A is heat transfer area, and LMTD is logarithmic mean temperature difference. For a given Q, as U decreases due to fouling, LMTD must increase. The normalized LMTD change rate (ΔLMTD/Δt)/P, where P is compressor power, provides a sensitivity metric that amplifies the fouling signal. Magnitude verification: A 0.0005 K/(W·day) threshold corresponds to approximately 0.15% daily efficiency loss, which accumulates to 3% in 20 days, meeting the constraint.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: 1) BMS data historian with timestamped values for chilled water supply/return temp, condenser water supply/return temp, compressor power, pump speed, outdoor wet-bulb temp; 2) Standard industrial PC running Python or MATLAB; 3) Off-the-shell numerical computation libraries. Procedure: a) Calculate LMTD from condenser water temperatures and refrigerant saturation temperature (derived from condenser pressure via refrigerant properties table); b) Compute normalized LMTD change rate using 24-hour rolling windows; c) Compare against threshold. No new hardware required; all computation uses existing logged data with standard heat transfer calculations.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Installability: SAME (uses existing BMS points, no new hardware). Operability: SAME (runs as background calculation, no operator interface changes). Maintenance: SAME (standard data historian maintenance, no additional burden). Cost: SAME (computation occurs on existing infrastructure). The burden is identical to standard practice, but provides earlier detection of fouling need, avoiding wasted cleaning labor and reducing energy consumption by at least 3% through optimized cleaning timing.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: 1) Install the algorithm on a test chiller; 2) Run for 30 days with known fouling simulation (gradually reducing condenser water flow rate to simulate fouling); 3) Compare cleaning triggers against actual fouling state. Instruments: BMS data historian, flow meter for validation. Pass threshold: Algorithm triggers cleaning when fouling causes ≥3% energy penalty versus fixed cadence, with detection within 3 days of fouling onset. Duration: 30-day test period. Kill criterion: If algorithm fails to detect fouling within 3 days or fails to achieve ≥3% energy savings compared to fixed monthly cleaning, the predictor is falsified.
